text: My brothers, not many of you should become teachers, for you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.
We all stumble in many ways. Anyone who never stumbles in what he says is mature, able to keep his whole body in check.
Think of horses: we put a bit in their mouths to make them obey us, and so we guide their whole body.
Or think of ships: however large they are, and however fierce the winds that drive them, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot wishes.
So it is with the tongue. It is a small part of the body, yet it makes great boasts. Consider how a little fire sets a great forest ablaze.

And the tongue is a fire. Among the parts of our body the tongue stands as a whole world of injustice; it stains the entire body, sets the whole course of our life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.*

versions.text: And the tongue is a fire. Among the parts of our body the tongue stands as a whole world of injustice; it stains the entire body, sets the whole course of our life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.
versions.explanation: Consider adding a footnote: "Greek: Gehenna, the valley outside Jerusalem that became an image of final judgment." This helps hearers understand the term without changing the readable text.

text: Every kind of animal and bird, every reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by humankind,
but no one can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who have been made in God's likeness.
Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be.
Does a spring pour out both fresh and bitter water from the same opening?
My brothers, can a fig tree bear olives, or a grapevine figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.
Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show it by a good life, by deeds done in the gentleness that wisdom brings.

versions.text: Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show it by his good way of life, in works done with the humility that comes from wisdom.
versions.explanation: The current clause is heavy for oral reading ("by his good way of life, in works done with..."), and πραΰτης is more precisely "gentleness/meekness" than "humility."

text: But if you harbor bitter envy and selfish ambition in your hearts, stop boasting and lying against the truth.
Such wisdom does not come down from above; it is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.
For where there is envy and selfish ambition, there you find disorder and every kind of evil.
But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, considerate, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.

versions.text: But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, considerate, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere.
versions.explanation: καρπῶν ἀγαθῶν is plural; "good fruits" better reflects the Greek and avoids confusion with the singular "fruit of righteousness" in verse 18.

text: And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

versions.text: And the harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
versions.explanation: "Harvest ... is sown" is a mixed metaphor (a harvest is reaped, not sown). The Greek καρπός here is better rendered "fruit," which keeps the agricultural image coherent and reads smoothly aloud.
